summary: Syed Ameer Ali was an Indian historian and religious studies scholar. He studied at Aliah University and the University of Calcutta (c. 1867–1869), where he later held a post from around 1873 to 1881.

Syed Hasan Askari was a scholar in history, archaeology, and Indology. Educated at Zila School Chapra, Langat Singh College, and Patna University, he succeeded Anant Sadashiv Altekar as Director of the K. P. Jayaswal Research Institute (1968–1971).
Syed Nawab Ali worked in history and archaeology. In 1932, he was attested as Professor of Persian at the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda and as Principal of Bahauddin College.
Sylvain Brocquet is a scholar in Indology and linguistics. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure in 1980 under Marie-Claude Porcher and held a post at Aix-Marseille University around 1999.

Sylvain Lévi specialized in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at the Sorbonne under Abel Bergaigne, later holding posts at the EPHE (1885–1935), Collège de France (1890–1935), and Maison Franco-Japonaise (1926–1928).

Sylvie Hureau works in Sinology and Buddhist studies. She held a position as maître de conférences at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (attested 2012) and as a Research Fellow at the International Institute for Buddhist Studies (attested 2026).

Sze-bong Tso is a scholar in Buddhist studies and Sinology. He earned his PhD at the Australian National University (1977–1982), where he studied under doctoral supervisors Jan Willem de Jong and Tissa Rajapatirana.

Sámuel Brassai was a scholar of linguistics, Indology, and philosophy. Educated at János Zsigmond Unitarian Highschool, he served at the John Sigismund Unitarian Academy (from 1837), Ludovika Military Academy (1848), and Franz Joseph University (1872–1884).

Sándor Kégl was an Indologist and Iranian and Central Asian studies scholar. He completed his PhD at Eötvös Loránd University under Ignác Goldziher and Ármin Vámbéry, later serving there as PD of Persian from 1893.

Sándor Kőrösi Csoma was a scholar of Tibetology and linguistics. He studied at Bethlen Gábor College, the University of Göttingen, and with traditional teachers in Tibet, later serving as Librarian at The Asiatic Society in the 1830s and 1840s.
Søren Ludvig Tuxen attended the Østre Borgerdyd school until 1868 and subsequently held a post there in 1875.

Søren Sørensen was an Indologist and linguist who earned his PhD at the University of Copenhagen under Johan Nicolai Madvig and Niels Ludvig Westergaard. He worked at Herlufsholm School (1876–1878) and Copenhagen (Docent, 1899).
Sāmaṇera Bodhesako worked in the field of Buddhist studies. He founded Path Press and served as an editor at the Buddhist Publication Society.
Sīlaratano studied under Narada Maha Thera, Nyanaponika Thera, and Ajahn Maha Bua (c. 1977–2011).

T. Chandrasekharan was an Indologist who studied under S. Kuppuswami Sastri. He served as Professor of History of Sanskrit Language and Literature at Madras Sanskrit College (attested 1951), where he succeeded T. R. Chintamani.

T. Ganapati Sastri was an Indologist who received a PhD from the University of Tübingen in 1924. From around 1908 to 1926, he served as Curator and Editor of the Travancore and Trivandrum Sanskrit Series.

T. Griffith Foulk studied Buddhist studies, Japanology, and Sinology, completing his PhD at the University of Michigan under Luis Oscar Gómez. He held faculty posts at Michigan (1987–1995) and Sarah Lawrence College (c. 1995–2015).
T. K. V. Desikachar worked in Indology, religious studies, and philosophy. He studied under Tirumalai Krishnamacharya from around 1961 to 1989 and founded the Krishnamacharya Yoga Mandiram in 1976.

T. N. Ramachandran was an Indian scholar in archaeology and Indology. He served as an archaeologist at the Government Museum, Chennai (c. 1925–1935) and as curator of archaeology at the National Museum, New Delhi.

T. R. Chintamani was an Indologist who earned his PhD at the University of Madras under S. Kuppuswami Sastri. He worked at the Adyar Library and Research Centre (c. 1928–1930) and Madras as Senior Lecturer in Sanskrit (1933).
